::: {.summary-section}
## Coarse graining a multipartite state

A multipartite quantum state can be viewed at different resolutions. Four laboratories may be treated separately, or two may be grouped into a single laboratory. The underlying state does not change, but the distinction between correlations inside a party and correlations between parties does. A measure intended to capture multipartite entanglement should respond meaningfully to this change of perspective. This paper investigates the proposal that a family of measures should not increase when parties are merged: **monotonicity under coarse graining**.

The proposal concerns pure states and a family called Rényi multi-entropies. It complements local-unitary invariance, symmetry between parties, and additivity for independent product states. The desired ordering for a general family of measures is:


$$
\displaystyle{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\Psi\rangle)-{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\Psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\geq 0\qquad\quad\forall\,{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}.
$$


The bracketed subscript means that two Hilbert-space factors are now regarded as one party. Repeated mergers generate many inequalities, organized by the partial order of partitions of the original parties. Thus the conjecture is a hierarchy rather than a single three-party comparison. An inequality for one merger can constrain every route through which a finely partitioned system is reduced to a coarser description.

Coarse graining changes which operations count as local: a joint unitary on the merged party can scramble degrees of freedom that previously belonged to separate laboratories. Local-unitary invariance makes the coarser measure insensitive to this scrambling. The proposed ordering therefore compares correlations resolved at two different scales within the same pure state. This gives a concrete counterpart to the familiar intuition that combining parties hides some of the multipartite structure.
:::

::: {.summary-section}
## Replica lattices and several routes to evidence

The construction begins with a polynomial local-unitary invariant: copies of the wavefunction and its complex conjugate are contracted with permutation-defined patterns. For Rényi multi-entropy the permutations are lattice translations, and the contraction can be drawn as a periodic lattice. Figure 1 shows a connected component of the three-party example. Its directions represent different parties, so identifying parties changes the contraction geometry in a controlled way.

![Figure 1. A connected component of the invariant obtained by choosing three independent generators of $\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ for the three party permutations. ([arXiv:2308.16247](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16247v1#S1.F3))](../assets/papers/2308.16247/q3_3_3.png){fig-alt="A connected periodic contraction network for a three-party invariant, with colored edges showing the three independent permutation directions."}

The Rényi multi-entropy is a logarithm of that invariant with a normalization depending on the number of parties. It is defined by:


$$
\displaystyle S_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}:=\frac{1}{1-n}\frac{1}{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-2}}{\rm log}({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}).
$$


This normalization is necessary when comparing descriptions with different numbers of parties. It also makes the entropy additive for independent tensor-product states, since their polynomial invariants multiply. Where the logarithm is defined, the entropy ordering has an equivalent formulation directly in terms of polynomial invariants. This polynomial form is useful for analytic proofs and numerical tests:


$$
\displaystyle{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\geq{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad{\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\leq\Big({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\Big)^{n}.
$$


Several complementary calculations then probe this assertion. Perturbation theory around factorized density matrices verifies it to second order, where the comparison reduces to controlled quadratic expressions. For classical probability distributions, regarded as diagonal density matrices of a purification, the proof uses inequalities between positive coefficients. Generalized three-party W states give another analytic test with genuinely quantum correlations. In that example the replica contraction can be reorganized as a lattice problem and related to a dimer model.

![Figure 2. Resolution of the four-valent density matrix in the lattice representation of the W-state invariant. ([arXiv:2308.16247](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16247v1#S4.F8))](../assets/papers/2308.16247/resolution.png){fig-alt="Graphical resolution of a four-valent density-matrix vertex into lower-valence pieces, used to reorganize the W-state contraction."}

The calculations are supplemented by numerical tests of randomly selected finite-dimensional states with several party numbers, dimensions, and replica indices. Agreement across these examples is evidence for the conjecture, while each analytic argument has its stated domain. The variety matters: diagonal states, small perturbations, W states, and random states probe different aspects of the same contraction inequality rather than repeating one special calculation.


:::

::: {.summary-section}
## Holographic monotonicity and saturation

A holographic argument supplies a geometrical perspective at replica index two. Under the brane-web prescription, merging parties removes interfaces between the corresponding bulk chambers. The cone parameter on an interface is continuously reduced until that singular segment disappears. The gravitational action responds according to a Schläfli-type formula. The action derivative takes the form:


$$
\displaystyle\partial_{n}S({\widetilde{\cal B}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{2}})})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A({\cal W}).
$$


Its positive-area right-hand side controls the direction of change. The method connects an information-theoretic inequality to the response of a hyperbolic cone geometry, provided the relevant saddle and continuation satisfy the geometric assumptions.

For a general multipartite state, this ordering is the monotonicity conjecture. The analytic proofs establish it for the stated classes, and the numerical tests explore systems with three, four, and five parties at several dimensions and replica indices. The polynomial formulation places these calculations in a common language: merging parties changes the contraction pattern, and the desired result compares the resulting homogeneous polynomials. Near a factorized state, the first-order terms saturate the comparison and the second-order terms determine the sign.

In the two-dimensional holographic setting at replica index two, the replica-symmetric cone-geometry prescription gives a direct realization of the merger operation. Each chamber touches a specified boundary region. The wall between two chambers disappears when its cone parameter reaches one, leaving precisely the coarser partition. Integrating the positive action derivative compares the two configurations. If the chambers already share no separating wall, the geometry remains unchanged and the coarse-graining inequality is saturated.

Saturation offers a way to identify which correlations a chosen merger removes. In the three-party examples, the discussion relates equality to factorization of the relevant reduced density matrix and to vanishing mutual information. In holography, equality can instead be read from the connectivity of the chamber decomposition. These complementary descriptions motivate multipartite versions of mutual information that diagnose correlations at different resolutions. They connect a proposed ordering of quantum states to a concrete question about which interfaces a gravitational geometry retains.
:::
